item.title: Hawkers need solutions beyond evictions. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-OSS-120B

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s directive to swiftly rehabilitate hawkers evicted from Dhaka’s streets is a necessary intervention in a problem that has dragged on for far too long. Hawkers are not criminals but workers, and a key part of our informal economy. When they are evicted without a plan, the consequences are immediate and severe. Creating a situation where they struggle to earn, or are forced to operate in unsafe or unsuitable locations, or pushed into debt, is not a solution. The PM’s words must therefore be treated as a directive to rethink how Dhaka handles its informal workforce. Hawkers need designated, well‑planned vending zones, not ad‑hoc spaces that shift with every police operation. They need clear rules, not arbitrary enforcement along with basic facilities so that their workplaces are dignified and safe. Most importantly, they need formal recognition so that their rights and responsibilities are defined rather than negotiated on the street. Cities around the world have shown that hawkers can coexist with traffic flow, pedestrian movement, and urban order, but only when the state plans for it. Dhaka’s current approach, built on periodic eviction drives that lead nowhere, has failed repeatedly. All such an approach has achieved is disrupted livelihoods, fueled tension, and ultimately, hawkers returning to the same spots out of necessity. Hawkers deserve stability, not uncertainty, with a system that acknowledges their role in the economy rather than treating them as obstacles to be removed. A proper solution therefore requires coordination to ensure that rehabilitation is practical, not symbolic. The PM has set the expectation. Now the administration must deliver.

item.title: Saving our tigers. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-OSS-20

The revelation that Bangladesh has only 189 tigers left should be treated for what it is - a national tragedy. The Royal Bengal Tiger is the most iconic species we have as a nation, it is quite literally the symbol of our natural heritage. That its numbers keep dwindling, and State Minister for Fisheries and Livestock Sultan Salauddin warning that the current situation is not sufficient to protect the species from extinction, is deeply concerning. When tiger numbers continue to fall, it signals deeper ecological distress that cannot be ignored. Experts have long cautioned that habitat loss, rising salinity, human encroachment, poaching, and climate‑driven changes in the Sundarbans are eroding the conditions tigers need to survive. The latest numbers only confirm that these pressures are intensifying. Conserving tigers should not be viewed as only about protecting a single species. It is about safeguarding the entire biodiversity of the Sundarbans - our most critical natural buffer against natural disasters such as cyclones and tidal surges. Bangladesh has taken steps: Strengthening patrols, expanding camera‑trap monitoring, and improving community engagement. However, it is plain to see that the scale of the challenge demands more. Conservation must be backed by sustained investment, scientific research, and strict enforcement against poaching and illegal resource extraction. The forest also needs better protection from industrial pressures, unregulated tourism, and climate impacts that are already reshaping its landscape. We must also broaden our focus beyond tigers. Biodiversity loss has been accelerating nationwide, from wetlands to hill forests to coastal ecosystems. Protecting wildlife therefore requires a holistic strategy, from restoring habitats to regulating development to integrating conservation into national planning rather than treating it as an isolated sector. The tiger population can recover, but only if we are able to act decisively, consistently, and with long‑term vision. Saving the tiger means saving the Sundarbans, and saving the Sundarbans means protecting our future.

item.title: Winning the fight against trafficking. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-OSS-20

Today is World Day Against Trafficking in Persons, and is a reminder that human trafficking remains one of the most persistent and damaging crimes. Every year, thousands of Bangladeshis fall victim to traffickers. Yet, trafficking is no longer confined to borders, brokers, or physical coercion. Much of it has moved online, and we are now facing a new generation of threats that exploit digital technology, social media, and the vulnerabilities of young people seeking opportunity. Human trafficking has always preyed on desperation. Today, it also preys on connectivity. Recruiters no longer need to visit villages or operate through local agents; they can reach victims through Facebook groups, messaging apps, job portals, and livestream platforms. From false job offers to fraudulent migration schemes, the digital shift has made trafficking faster, harder to detect, and easier to disguise as legitimate opportunity. For Bangladesh, this evolution is especially dangerous. Millions of young people are online, often without digital literacy or awareness of the risks. Migrant workers increasingly rely on social media for job information. Traffickers have adapted, and our protection systems must adapt with equal speed. Bangladesh has made progress in combating traditional trafficking routes, strengthening laws, and improving rescue and rehabilitation. But the digital dimension remains under-addressed. Law enforcement lacks specialized cyber‑trafficking units. Border and migration officials are not always trained to identify victims recruited online. And survivors often struggle to navigate the legal system when exploitation begins on a screen rather than at a border. On this day, the message is clear: Strengthening protection means also strengthening digital vigilance. Traffickers are online and Bangladesh must be ready to meet them there. Trafficking has changed and our response must change with it. We cannot rely on old tools to fight a new threat.

item.title: When childhood becomes the first casualty of climate change. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-OSS-20

There was a time when climate change in Bangladesh was discussed through the language of infrastructure. The conversation revolved around embankments, cyclone shelters, flood control projects, adaptation funds, and carbon emissions. Success was measured by the number of kilometres of embankments built or the amount of international climate finance secured. Children appeared in these discussions only as passive victims to be rescued after disaster struck. The latest Children’s Climate Risk Report 2026 by Unicef demands that we abandon that habit of thinking. It suggests something far more unsettling. Bangladesh is not merely fighting a climate crisis. It is slowly becoming a place where childhood itself is being reshaped by an environment that is growing increasingly hostile. This is perhaps the most important lesson hidden beneath the report’s alarming statistics. Climate change is no longer only about damaged roads, submerged villages or destroyed crops. It is altering what it means to grow up in Bangladesh. The report places Bangladesh fourth among the countries where children face the highest climate risks, with an overall vulnerability score of 9.38 out of 10. Only Myanmar, Pakistan, and Vietnam rank higher. Bangladesh receives the maximum possible risk score, 10 out of 10, for riverine flooding, making its children the most exposed in the world to this particular hazard. The country’s scores remain alarmingly high across nearly every category, including tropical cyclones at 9.7, air pollution at 9.7, drought at 9.65, extreme heat at 9.24, and coastal flooding at 8.13. These numbers are disturbing enough. Yet the real story lies in what they collectively reveal. Climate disasters rarely arrive one at a time anymore. Bangladesh increasingly experiences overlapping emergencies where one hazard begins before another has fully disappeared. Floods are followed by disease outbreaks. Cyclones are followed by prolonged displacement. Heatwaves arrive before communities recover from previous disasters. Air pollution quietly intensifies throughout the year, affecting children even when skies appear clear. The report captures this reality by arguing that Bangladeshi children are exposed not to isolated disasters but to multiple climate shocks simultaneously. Nearly 60 million children in Bangladesh are exposed to at least one climate-related hazard. More than 24 million face the combined risks of floods, droughts, and cyclones. Around 32 million children are directly threatened by riverine flooding, about 22 million by cyclones, while roughly 60 million are exposed to drought and air pollution. These figures are difficult to comprehend because they describe an entire generation rather than isolated communities. The tendency is often to think of climate change through dramatic images of flooded villages or collapsing riverbanks. Those images matter, but they obscure a slower crisis unfolding inside classrooms, hospitals, and homes. When schools become shelters after cyclones, education stops. When repeated flooding destroys family income, children become workers instead of students. When prolonged displacement breaks community networks, girls become more vulnerable to early marriage while boys face greater pressure to enter informal labour markets. Health deteriorates because clean drinking water becomes scarce, sanitation systems collapse and disease spreads more easily. The damage extends well beyond the immediate disaster. A child who misses several months of education today may experience lower earnings decades later. A malnourished infant exposed to repeated climate shocks may never fully recover physically or cognitively. Psychological trauma caused by repeated disasters often remains invisible, although it shapes behaviour and emotional well-being for years. These are losses that no disaster compensation package can fully repair. One of the most overlooked findings in the Unicef report is that Bangladesh actually performs comparatively better in several traditional child development indicators such as child health, nutrition, education, poverty reduction, and maternal mortality. In other words, the country has made genuine progress over the past decades. Yet climate change threatens to reverse those achievements. The environmental conditions necessary to sustain these gains are becoming increasingly unstable. Development successes built over decades now stand on uncertain ecological foundations. Perhaps this explains why conventional adaptation strategies increasingly appear insufficient. Much of Bangladesh’s climate planning understandably focuses on physical infrastructure. Cyclone shelters save lives. Embankments reduce flood damage. River dredging improves water management. These remain essential investments. However, the next stage of adaptation requires a different question. Instead of asking how infrastructure survives climate change, policy-makers must ask how childhood survives climate change. These are not identical questions. Children experience disasters differently from adults because their bodies, minds, and futures are still developing. A week without school affects an eight-year-old differently than it affects a thirty-year-old office worker. Air pollution permanently damages developing lungs more severely than adult lungs. Malnutrition during childhood produces lifelong consequences that cannot simply be reversed later. The report estimates that around 337 million children worldwide face riverine flooding, 662 million face tropical storms, 33 million are exposed to coastal flooding, approximately 1.2 billion experience extreme heat and nearly 1.8 billion face drought. Around 80% of children exposed to riverine and coastal flooding live in only 10 countries, with Bangladesh among the most heavily affected. These global figures remind us that Bangladesh occupies the frontline of a worldwide crisis. Yet unlike wealthier nations, Bangladesh must confront this emergency while still addressing poverty, rapid urbanization, infrastructure deficits, and demographic pressures. This makes policy choices especially important. Climate adaptation cannot remain concentrated only within environment ministries. It must become the organizing principle across education, public health, urban planning, and social protection. A single national blueprint cannot adequately protect them all. Floating schools may be appropriate in flood-prone wetlands. Residential educational facilities may prove more effective in remote hill regions. Coastal districts require stronger shelter systems designed specifically around children’s needs. Urban schools increasingly need shaded environments capable of protecting students during prolonged heatwaves. Climate adaptation succeeds only when geography shapes policy. Equally important is recognizing that children are not merely recipients of protection. Young people increasingly understand climate risks because they experience them firsthand. Many already participate in community preparedness programs, environmental campaigns, and local adaptation initiatives. Their perspectives often reveal practical problems adults overlook. Treating children solely as vulnerable populations ignores their potential as active participants in building resilience. Unicef rightly argues that children should be meaningfully included in climate policy-making. This is not symbolic participation. It reflects the reality that today’s policy decisions will define their entire futures far more than they will affect current decision-makers. There is also an uncomfortable issue the international community cannot continue avoiding. Bangladeshi children contribute almost nothing to global greenhouse gas emissions. Yet they bear some of the world’s highest climate risks. This remains one of the greatest moral failures of modern international politics. The countries and populations least responsible for warming the planet continue paying its highest human costs. Climate justice therefore cannot remain confined to abstract diplomatic language during international summits. It must translate into predictable adaptation finance, technology transfer, and long-term investments focused specifically on children’s well-being. HM Nazmul Alam is an Academic, Journalist, and Political Analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

“Consular officers may require covered nonimmigrant visa applicants to post a bond of up to $20,000 as a condition of visa issuance, as determined by the consular officers,” the notice said.

A correctional system that cannot care for those within it is not one that can be looked at in a positive light. This is a state of affairs that demands immediate correction. With that said, this development should be seen as part of a much larger national need: We have long needed to invest far more - and far more consistently - in our rail network. For decades, rail has been treated as a secondary mode of transport, overshadowed by highways and short‑term road expansion. The result is visible everywhere: Congested highways, unsafe long‑distance bus travel, rising transport emissions, and logistics bottlenecks that have slowed down our economy. Rail, by contrast, is safer, cleaner, more affordable, and far more efficient for both passengers and freight. As such, we expect the same urgency across all rail routes to all divisions. Freight corridors too must be strengthened so industries can move goods without relying solely on trucks. And regional links - including potential future connections with India, Nepal, and Bhutan - should be part of long‑term planning. Our ever-growing population and rising urbanization demand a transport system that can move people and goods reliably. Bangladesh has already invested heavily in megaprojects, sometimes unwisely. Now it must invest in the everyday infrastructure that keeps a country moving. The real goal should be clear: A modern, extensive, and reliable rail network that serves the entire nation.

item.title: Reviving our waterways. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-OSS-20

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s directive to take coordinated steps to curb pollution in Dhaka’s rivers, improve drainage, and ensure normal water flow by maintaining navigability is timely and goes straight to the heart of an all-too-familiar problem. Thus, while the government is deciding to allow interested private companies to operate water bus services on waterways around Dhaka, this initiative will mean little if the rivers themselves remain choked, polluted, and unnavigable. It is a shame how our capital’s waterways have continued to deteriorate; encroachment continues unchecked, industrial waste is not regulated, and drainage canals are clogged with plastic and construction debris. Introducing or enhancing our network of water transport thus requires reviving the waterways on which they will operate first. That means coordinated action -- not isolated, short‑term clean‑ups. To curb pollution, enforcement must be uncompromising while factories dumping untreated waste must face real penalties, not warnings. Encroachers must be removed permanently, not temporarily and drainage systems must be redesigned so the water actually flows into rivers without carrying urban garbage. Improving drainage is equally critical. Dhaka’s canals have been narrowed, filled, or built over, and we have seen how it has left the city vulnerable to waterlogging due to preventing natural water flow. Restoring these canals is therefore not just an environmental task but essential to improving our urban infrastructure. The High Court’s order for the disposal of all pending applications for new passports and passport renewals filed by Bangladeshi expatriates within 60 days is certainly a welcome intervention but also exposes a much larger, persistent problem. Whether it is passports, land records, utility services, welfare benefits, or any other basic documentation, our public service delivery, despite lofty exclamations of digitization and reform, remains slow, fragmented, and deeply frustrating for ordinary citizens. The expat passport backlog is only one symptom of a system that struggles to keep pace with the country’s growing population, rising mobility, and expanding digital expectations. When expatriates, who contribute billions in remittances, face delays of weeks or months for something as fundamental as a passport, we must call it what it is: A structural failure. The same inefficiencies affect millions at home: Long queues, opaque procedures, inconsistent timelines, and a lack of accountability. The High Court’s directive is therefore less a procedural order and more a reminder that public service delivery must be fast, predictable, and citizen‑centred. We are a nation that aspires to reach middle‑income efficiency but that is impossible with our present outdated administrative practices. The solution requires systemic reform, and it begins with those in charge actually caring about doing their jobs properly. Better coordination rather than operating in silos and digital systems that are fully integrated, not partially adopted, should be the minimum expectation. Citizens deserve to receive timely responses instead of bureaucratic runarounds. Public services are not favours but rights. A modern Bangladesh demands modern service delivery, one that is transparent, efficient, and accountable, serving the best interest of the people.

item.title: The July Revolution and the reinvention of national purpose. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-20

Every generation inherits a defining historical moment. Some inherit liberation wars. Others inherit economic transformations or constitutional crises. The generation of Bangladesh that came of age in 2024 inherited something different: A civic uprising that fundamentally challenged the relationship between the citizen and the state. Two years after the July Revolution, political debates continue over who deserves credit, who bears responsibility, and whose narrative should ultimately dominate history. Governments have changed. Political alignments have shifted. New actors have emerged while old ones have disappeared from power. Yet if the anniversary of the July uprising teaches Bangladesh anything, it should be this: The true significance of those days extends far beyond partisan politics. The revolution ultimately became a test of whether Bangladesh could place the interests of the republic above the interests of competing political forces. That is why "Bangladesh First" carries far greater significance than a patriotic slogan. It offers an opportunity to revisit July not simply as a political movement but as a national moment of introspection. The essential question is no longer who won or who lost. Rather, it is whether Bangladesh itself became stronger through the crisis, and whether the painful lessons of those weeks are being translated into stronger institutions, greater accountability, and a more mature democratic culture. History repeatedly demonstrates that nations are transformed not merely by revolutions but by the lessons they choose to remember afterwards. France remembers 1789 differently from 1793. The United States remembers the Civil Rights Movement not only through legislation but through its continuing struggle with equality. South Africa continues to reinterpret the end of apartheid through debates about justice, reconciliation, and institutional reform. Likewise, Bangladesh's July Revolution should not become frozen as a monument belonging to one political generation. It should remain an evolving national conversation about citizenship, state power, public accountability and democratic responsibility. The greatest danger for any nation after a transformative political event is the temptation to reduce history to heroes and villains alone. Such narratives are emotionally satisfying but intellectually incomplete. They rarely explain why events unfolded as they did or why ordinary citizens suddenly became willing to assume extraordinary risks. Bangladesh deserves a more mature conversation. The July Revolution did not emerge suddenly on August 5. Nor was it born exclusively from the quota issue. Rather, the quota movement became the catalyst through which years of accumulated public frustration found organized expression. Understanding that distinction is essential for understanding modern Bangladesh. The quota issue was never only about quotas When the High Court restored the freedom fighter quota on June 5, 2024, many observers initially treated it as another legal controversy in Bangladesh's long history of disputes over public recruitment. Viewed in isolation, the judgment concerned administrative policy. Viewed within the broader socio-economic context, however, it touched one of the deepest anxieties facing contemporary Bangladesh. The country's demographic reality had changed dramatically over the previous decade. Bangladesh successfully expanded access to higher education, producing hundreds of thousands of university graduates every year. Yet economic expansion did not generate public-sector employment opportunities at a comparable pace. For many young graduates, government employment represented not merely a career but economic security, social mobility, and dignity. Consequently, recruitment policies became deeply symbolic. They represented competing visions of fairness itself. Supporters of quotas argued that the Liberation War deserved institutional recognition and that the sacrifices of freedom fighters should continue receiving state acknowledgement. Their argument rested upon historical justice. Opponents did not necessarily reject that history. Rather, they questioned whether historical recognition should continue shaping recruitment in ways they believed constrained meritocracy in a rapidly changing society. Their concern centred upon contemporary fairness. Both positions possessed moral foundations. The problem emerged because the national conversation increasingly ceased to distinguish disagreement from hostility. Instead of facilitating constructive debate regarding balancing historical obligations with present realities, political discourse gradually became polarized between competing moral absolutes. Once that occurred, compromise became increasingly difficult. The events that followed therefore cannot be understood merely as reactions to one judicial verdict. They reflected a deeper institutional challenge confronting Bangladesh: How should a nation honour its history without allowing historical memory itself to become a source of contemporary division? That question remains relevant today. From administrative dispute to national conversation The earliest demonstrations following the June 5 verdict remained remarkably restrained. Students organized peaceful processions, submitted memoranda, and appealed to constitutional institutions. Even during the first weeks, their strategy demonstrated an important characteristic that is often overlooked in retrospective political narratives. The movement initially expressed confidence in the state rather than rejection of it. This distinction deserves emphasis. Citizens protest because they expect governments to listen. Only when they gradually lose confidence in institutional responsiveness do demonstrations begin acquiring broader political significance. The students' memorandum to the Attorney General, their repeated appeals before the scheduled Supreme Court hearing, and their insistence upon legal remedies all suggested that the movement still believed constitutional mechanisms could resolve the dispute. In many respects, this reflected democratic maturity rather than political confrontation. History often forgets this early phase because later violence overshadows earlier restraint. Yet remembering it matters because it reveals that Bangladesh's institutions initially possessed opportunities for de-escalation. Whether those opportunities were fully utilized remains a question historians will continue debating. Why the movement spread beyond Dhaka By the beginning of July, something fundamentally changed. The demonstrations no longer remained confined to Dhaka University. Students from public universities across Bangladesh joined under the banner of the Anti-Discrimination Student Movement. Within days, private universities also became increasingly engaged. Geographical expansion alone does not create a national movement. Shared emotional experience does. The speed with which the protests spread suggested that the quota issue had become a vessel carrying broader public frustrations. Across campuses, students increasingly interpreted the controversy as representing wider concerns regarding equality of opportunity, institutional responsiveness, youth unemployment and perceptions of exclusion. This phenomenon deserves careful analysis. Throughout modern history, transformative political movements rarely remain confined to their original grievances. The American Civil Rights Movement expanded beyond segregated buses. Poland's Solidarity movement grew beyond labour rights. The Arab Spring quickly moved beyond isolated acts of protest. Not because the original issues disappeared. Rather, because they revealed deeper structural frustrations already existing beneath the surface. Bangladesh followed a remarkably similar trajectory. The quota issue became the spark. The combustible material already existed. Perhaps no development illustrated this transformation more clearly than the emergence of the “Bangla blockade.” At first glance, blocking highways appears merely as another protest tactic. In reality, it represented an important shift in political strategy. Modern democracies are organized around shared public spaces. Roads, railway stations, bridges and major intersections connect citizens regardless of political affiliation or social class. Once those spaces become sites of political expression, the movement inevitably enters everyday national life. Until then, many Bangladeshis could observe events from a distance. The blockade made neutrality increasingly difficult. Office workers encountered demonstrations on their commute. Business owners experienced economic disruption. Parents worried about children travelling across cities. Citizens previously disengaged from politics suddenly found themselves participating emotionally because politics had entered their daily routines. Critics understandably questioned whether disrupting public life could ever be justified. Supporters argued that extraordinary institutional inaction required extraordinary civic pressure. Both arguments remain worthy of debate. However, irrespective of one's political position, the blockade undeniably succeeded in transforming a student protest into a national conversation. That strategic transformation proved historically decisive. The crisis of institutional communication One of the most revealing aspects of the early weeks was not the demonstrations themselves but the widening gap between institutional language and public perception. The government largely approached the situation through administrative and legal frameworks. Officials repeatedly emphasized that the matter remained before the courts and therefore required judicial resolution. Constitutionally, such reasoning appeared sound. Politically, however, it increasingly failed to resonate with protesters. This disconnect reflected a broader challenge confronting modern governance. Institutions often respond to procedural questions while citizens increasingly raise emotional ones. Governments speak about jurisdiction. Citizens speak about justice. Governments discuss legal timelines. Citizens measure political responsiveness. Neither conversation is necessarily incorrect. The problem emerges when neither side recognizes the legitimacy of the other's concerns. Bangladesh experienced precisely that communication breakdown. Each successive day widened the psychological distance between state institutions and student expectations. Once such gaps become sufficiently large, even well-intentioned policy responses struggle to restore confidence. Trust, after all, is far easier to lose than to rebuild. The politics of language Every political movement eventually encounters a symbolic moment that transforms its emotional character. For Bangladesh, that moment arrived on July 14. Until then, the movement had largely centred upon policy. Following the prime minister's remarks concerning " razakars ," the national conversation changed almost overnight. Political language matters because words do more than communicate.They define identity. The slogan that subsequently echoed across university campuses was not significant merely because it spread rapidly. Its deeper significance lay in how protesters transformed an accusation into satire. Throughout history, satire has often become one of the most powerful instruments of political resistance because it deprives authority of its monopoly over language. The July slogan demonstrated precisely that phenomenon. Whether one approved of the slogan or not, its impact upon public consciousness became undeniable. The movement was no longer debating administrative policy. It had entered the far more emotionally charged territory of dignity, recognition, and national identity. Once political conflicts become struggles over dignity rather than policy, compromise becomes significantly more difficult. Bangladesh was approaching that threshold. The first 40 days of the July Revolution therefore reveal a truth that should remain central to any honest historical assessment. Contrary to many later political interpretations, the movement did not begin as a campaign to overthrow a government. It began as an appeal for institutional responsiveness within the constitutional framework. Only gradually, through successive failures of communication, growing polarization, expanding public participation, and escalating confrontation, did it evolve into something much larger. Understanding that evolution matters because it contains perhaps the most important lesson for contemporary Bangladesh. Nations are rarely destabilized by one controversial decision alone. They are destabilized when institutions fail to recognize how individual decisions accumulate into broader crises of public confidence. For every future government -- regardless of ideology -- that may be the most enduring lesson of June and early July 2024. The republic is always strongest when citizens believe they can be heard before they feel compelled to be remembered. HM Nazmul Alam is an Academic, Journalist, and Political Analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.
